https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday ordered a three-day halt to strikes on Kyiv as U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow hoping to restart stalled negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. Kyiv had previously proposed a ceasefire ahead of the diplomatic talks. “Indeed, such information was received from the Ukrainian side. Russian President and Commander-in-Chief Putin gave orders to hold off on attacks on Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” Moscow press secretary Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Saturday. Advertisement Advertisement “This is due to the preparation and conduct of American contacts in Kyiv,” Peskov said. Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to the Ukrainian capital on Sunday. Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent weeks . Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up its hits on Russia’s oil infrastructure, in August reaching a monthly record for strikes since the start of the war in 2022. Saturday’s pause order followed a broad Russian overnight attack across Ukraine that killed at least five people and injured six others, according to the Kyiv Independent . “They were deliberate, for the first time in a long while,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram of the strikes targeting airports in Kyiv and Boryspil. “Clearly, Russia’s strikes on the airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations concerning the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine.” The U.S. emissaries are scheduled to meet with Putin later on Saturday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3.text: Image source, Getty Image caption, PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world" By Lana Lam Sydney Published 9 hours ago Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack. In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack. On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks. AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology". "The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said. One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence . This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm". The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks. This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach. In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent . OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September. It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told. Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI. Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.
